# The Rector of Justin

## Lead

The Rector of Justin is a novel by American writer Louis Auchincloss, first published by Houghton Mifflin in 1964. The book centers on the life and leadership of a celebrated headmaster at an elite New England boarding school and examines the moral and institutional dimensions of American upper-class education and culture. Contemporary critics praised the novel; The New York Times described it on December 4, 1964, as “the best novel of the year” and “a subtle, ironic and compassionate story about a celebrated schoolmaster.” The Rector of Justin was a bestseller in 1964 and was a finalist for the National Book Award in Fiction in 1965. It has often been cited as Auchincloss’s most acclaimed work, including by The New York Times in a December 15, 2010 assessment of his memoir, which referred to The Rector of Justin (1964) as his “best and most celebrated novel.” 

## Background and composition

Louis Auchincloss (born September 27, 1917; died January 26, 2010) was a prolific American novelist, short-story writer, and critic best known for novels of manners set in the world of corporate boardrooms and upper-class New York. His work is noted for stylistic clarity and characterization, often focused on formative influences and personal limitations rather than sensational excesses. The Rector of Justin fits into his broader interest in the institutions and leaders of the American elite, depicting a boarding school headmaster and the moral claims of educational leadership.

While detailed accounts of Auchincloss’s drafting process for The Rector of Justin are not widely available in primary sources accessible online, contemporaneous and retrospective criticism positions the book as a culminating example of his institutional novel, drawing on his social knowledge of elite educational environments to explore character, authority, and the ethos of leadership. The book’s emphasis on the American establishment and educational leadership has been analyzed in discussions of schooling and governance, including commentary on its enduring relevance to debates about teaching and institutional reform. 

## Setting and narrative structure

The novel is set in and around a prestigious New England boys’ boarding school and centers on the long career of its headmaster. Reviews and critical commentary describe a narrative that builds a many-sided portrait of a “celebrated schoolmaster,” rendering his ideals, compromises, and the institutional culture in which he operates. Although detailed structural descriptions vary by critic, accounts emphasize the novel’s multi-perspective approach to the headmaster’s life and legacy, situating the narrative within the traditions of the American institutional and “school” novel. 

## Plot summary

The Rector of Justin follows the rise, authority, and later years of a renowned boarding-school headmaster and the evolution of the school he leads. Through accounts that reflect the views of those around him (students, colleagues, admirers, and skeptics), the novel traces the headmaster’s educational ideals, his methods of moral instruction, and the institutional pressures he navigates. The story develops a nuanced portrait that balances admiration with critical scrutiny, culminating in an assessment of his legacy—what he achieved, where he compromised, and how his leadership shaped generations. 

## Principal characters

Reliable sources describe the novel’s focus on the headmaster and those within his institutional orbit. Contemporary reviews emphasize a portrait of “a celebrated schoolmaster,” with observers whose viewpoints contribute to the characterization and moral argument of the book. Subsequent discussions of the novel’s continuing relevance in education policy literature point to the headmaster’s role as a model for leadership ideals, with interlocutors who reflect on teaching, discipline, and institutional mission. Publicly accessible, high-quality sources do not enumerate a comprehensive character list with full names; critical descriptions instead center on roles and relationships within the school.

## Themes and analysis

- Leadership and moral authority in elite institutions: Critics have highlighted the novel’s exploration of authority—how a leader articulates ideals, exercises power, and mentors youth—and the tension between personal conviction and institutional constraints. The New York Times characterized the narrative as compassionate and ironic, suggesting a balanced depiction that avoids simple heroization. 

- The American upper class and establishment culture: Auchincloss’s oeuvre is widely associated with the manners and mores of the upper class; The Rector of Justin extends that focus to the educational institutions that reproduce elite norms. Analyses of the novel in education-policy contexts interpret it as a source of reflections on teaching, discipline, and institutional mission with continuing relevance to modern reforms. 

- Institutional power and the shaping of character: The book situates education as a formative sphere where institutional values and personal leadership shape students’ identities and futures, raising questions about tradition, change, and the ethical responsibilities of authority figures. 

## Publication history and editions

- First edition: The Rector of Justin was published by Houghton Mifflin in 1964. A bibliographic record indicates the first edition comprised 341 pages and was produced with Riverside Press (Cambridge, Mass.) as contributor; the Google Books bibliographic entry provides page count and publisher details for the 1964 edition. The publication year 1964 is also reflected in library records compiled by HathiTrust. 

- Identifiers: A widely used WorldCat record for the 1964 edition carries OCLC number 279743. 

- Reprints: The novel has been reissued; a National Book Foundation catalog entry for the title lists ISBN 978-0618224890 for a Mariner Books | Houghton Mifflin Company edition, and identifies Boston as place of publication. Publicly accessible publisher pages for all later reprints are not fully consolidated online; however, the National Book Foundation record confirms the Mariner reprint ISBN.

## Reception

Contemporaneous reception was strongly positive. The New York Times “Books of The Times” column on December 4, 1964 praised The Rector of Justin as “the best novel of the year,” calling it “a subtle, ironic and compassionate story about a celebrated schoolmaster.” On December 6, 1964, the Times published a publishing-industry column noting a regret by one editor that another house rather than his had published “one absolutely splendid book, ‘The Rector of Justin’.” 

Later assessments reinforced the book’s standing. In a December 4, 1994 review of Auchincloss’s work, The New York Times described The Rector of Justin as his “splendid 1964 best seller” and noted it had been “nominated for major prizes,” giving emphasis to its distinct critical and commercial position within his oeuvre. In a December 15, 2010 review, The New York Times referred to The Rector of Justin (1964) as Auchincloss’s “best and most celebrated novel.” 

## Awards and honors

The Rector of Justin was a finalist for the National Book Award in Fiction for the 1965 awards cycle. The National Book Foundation’s official 1965 awards page lists Saul Bellow’s Herzog as the winner and includes The Rector of Justin among the finalists. 

## Sales and impact

The novel was a bestseller in 1964, as described in The New York Times’s retrospective discussion of Auchincloss’s career. Education policy commentary in Education Next emphasizes the book’s enduring relevance for reflections on teaching and school leadership, noting its status as a best seller and National Book Award finalist and remarking on its reputation among critics as one of Auchincloss’s best works. The book’s influence in discussions of American elite education and the moral imperatives of leadership has been noted by critics across decades. 

## Adaptations

Publicly accessible, high-quality sources do not document film, television, or stage adaptations of The Rector of Justin. Library and publisher records primarily reflect print publication and later reprints. 

## Legacy

The Rector of Justin is frequently singled out as Louis Auchincloss’s signature novel. The New York Times in 2010 called it his “best and most celebrated novel.” Within surveys of Auchincloss’s career, The Rector of Justin is often cited as a high point for his exploration of institutional power and elite culture, combining his characteristic stylistic clarity with a complex portrait of leadership and moral authority within American education.

THE COLLECTED STORIES OF LOUIS AUCHINCLOSS 465 pp. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company. $24.95.

FORTY-SEVEN years and 50 books after he published his first novel, "The Indifferent Children," Louis Auchincloss has yet to receive his full due. Academic critics and editors of anthologies have almost completely ignored him; so have the bestowers of literary awards. (Of all his books, only the splendid 1964 best seller "The Rector of Justin" has been nominated for major prizes.)

Why is this? The complaints are remarkably consistent: Mr. Auchincloss focuses on too tiny a sliver of human society -- namely, the world of upper-crust New York WASP's, especially white-shoe Wall Street lawyers (of which he is one) -- and treats his material in an old-fashioned manner that is overly derivative of Edith Wharton and Henry James. But these charges are outrageously unfair.

Yes, Mr. Auchincloss's social-register characters and stately prose often bring Wharton and James to mind; for some of us, that is not an unpleasant experience. Unfortunately for Mr. Auchincloss, he lives in a time when the protagonists of literary fiction tend to be middle- or lower-class, when the rich and powerful (in the form of movie stars and self-made tycoons) are found mostly in Jackie Collins-style potboilers, when both popular culture and serious fiction have propagated the notion that Ivy League Episcopalian types are emotionless snobs.

These days the general public, though fascinated by the superficial trappings of privilege, seems to have little interest in the deeper truths with which Mr. Auchincloss is passionately concerned -- with, that is, the beliefs, principles, hypocrisies, prejudices and assorted strengths and defects of character that typify the American WASP civilization that produced what was for a long time the country's undisputed ruling class. Mr. Auchincloss may concentrate on a limited milieu, but it is a milieu whose impact on American society has been immense and whose decline in influence has been intimately connected to some of the most significant social changes of recent decades. It is a milieu, one might add, that Mr. Auchincloss knows intimately, and of which he is at once a sincere eulogist and a trenchant critic.

Few of Mr. Auchincloss's books demonstrate this fact as surely as "The Collected Stories of Louis Auch incloss," his third to be published this year -- and one that shows some of Mr. Auchincloss's best work in his strongest genre. Several of the earliest stories here -- there are 19 in all, the oldest dating back to the late 1940's -- view Mr. Auchincloss's little world through the eyes of characters who inhabit it but who are, in some way, outsiders. Both "Greg's Peg" and "The Single Reader," for example, are about friendless bachelors: one finds his niche as the local buffoon in a summer beach town; the other keeps a voluminous diary about the elite circles in which he moves, observing everything but never really participating. Mr. Auchincloss shows off his sense of humor in "The Colonel's Foundation," an eminently anthologizable little tale about a misfit lawyer who foolishly leaps at an apparent opportunity that his wiser colleagues would flatly reject, and in "The Mavericks," wherein an Irish-American lawyer's bluntness wins him the affection of his boss's unconventional daughter.

The theme of not belonging figures pivotally in the book's two most impressive stories, both of which were first collected in "The Romantic Egoists" (1954). "The Gemlike Flame" brilliantly delineates the complex, ambiguous relationship between Clarence, a reclusive American esthete in Venice, and Neddy, a male artist who becomes his protege and (as Clarence puts it) the object of his "pure love." The situation strongly recalls James's novel "Roderick Hudson"; the narrator's description of Clarence as Neddy's "preceptor," furthermore, seems calculated to stir memories of James's story "The Pupil," in which that word occurs repeatedly.

**Louis Auchincloss** (born September 27, 1917, Lawrence, [New York](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-state), U.S.—died January 26, 2010, [New York City](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-York-City)) was an American novelist, short-story writer, and critic, best known for his novels of manners set in the world of contemporary upper-class New York City.

Auchincloss studied at [Yale University](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Yale-University) from 1935 to 1939 and graduated from the [University of Virginia](https://www.britannica.com/topic/University-of-Virginia) Law School in 1941. He was admitted to the New York state bar that same year and began a legal career that would last until 1986.

For his first [novel](https://www.britannica.com/art/novel), _The Indifferent Children_ (1947), Auchincloss used the pseudonym Andrew Lee, but by 1950 he was publishing stories under his own name. Noted for his stylistic clarity and skill at characterization, he became the [prolific](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/prolific) chronicler of life in the rarefied world of corporate boardrooms and brownstone mansions. As a novelist, Auchincloss was less interested in the excesses and intrigues of his characters than he was in their formative influences and personal limitations.

Several of his best novels, including _The House of Five Talents_ (1960) and _Portrait in Brownstone_ (1962), examine family relationships over a period of decades. Others, notably _The Rector of Justin_ (1964) and _Diary of a Yuppie_ (1987), are studies of a single character, often from many points of view. Auchincloss frequently linked the stories in his collections by theme or geography, as in, for example, _Tales of Manhattan_ (1967) and _Skinny Island_ (1987), which are set exclusively in Manhattan. Subsequent works include the novels _Tales of Yesteryear_ (1994) and _Education of Oscar Fairfax_ (1995) and a number of short-story anthologies, notably _Three Lives_ (1993), _The Anniversary and Other Stories_ (1999), and _Manhattan Monologues_ (2002), all of which explore [moral](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/moral) dilemmas of the upper class. Without straying far from the world of the wealthy, Auchincloss published _Her Infinite Variety_ (2000), a novel set in 1930s New York about a woman fighting her way up the social ladder, and _The Scarlet Letters_ (2003), a moral fable set in contemporary [New England](https://www.britannica.com/place/New-England). _East Side Story_ (2004) is loosely based on Auchincloss’s father’s family. Two more short-story collections followed these novels; then, at the age of 90, Auchincloss published _The Headmaster’s Dilemma_ (2007), a novel about a noble headmaster at a New England [prep school](https://www.britannica.com/topic/preparatory-school).

Books of The Times

A Man Who Knew the People Who Mattered, and Wrote About Them
------------------------------------------------------------

*   Dec. 14, 2010

When the novelist Louis Auchincloss [died](http://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/28/nyregion/28auchincloss.html?_r=1&scp=1&sq=auchincloss%20obituary&st=cse "New York Times obituary") last January, at 92, his timing could hardly have been worse. J. D. Salinger died the next day, obliterating much of the attention that would have come Auchincloss’s way. To put it in Holden Caulfield’s words, “People never notice anything.”

Nearly a year after his death and almost 50 years since he wrote his best and most celebrated novel, [“The Rector of Justin”](http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2008/07/08/AR2008070802729.html "Washington Post essay on book") (1964), Auchincloss remains a difficult writer to get a handle on.

The rap against his work is clear enough. It’s that he wrote too much of it (more than 60 books, while also practicing law) and focused too relentlessly on the insular world he was born into: New York’s elite old families. His great subject was the effect  both warming and warping  of wealth and its neurotic cousin, social class.

Auchincloss fired back, skillfully enough, at the critics who found his work narrow. “That business of objecting to the subject material or the people that an author writes about is purely class prejudice,” he told an interviewer in 1997, “and you will note that it always disappears with an author’s death. Nobody holds it against Henry James or Edith Wharton or Thackeray or Marcel Proust.”

Yet Auchincloss, despite being an acute and feeling observer, isn’t a James or a Wharton. His work lacks electricity and sweep, and his dozens of novels bleed together in the mind. He’s a major minor writer who seems likely to be remembered, when he is, for just a small handful of books.

His posthumous memoir, “A Voice From Old New York: A Memoir of My Youth,” is unlikely to be among those volumes. It’s thin and episodic, and lacks a certain necessary friction. But it does provide a genuine taste of what makes Auchincloss so interesting a writer. It’s plainspoken and pays close attention to a certain disappearing brand of manners and morals. “A Voice From Old New York” is a peek into a rapidly vanishing world and into a determined writer’s coming of age.

Auchincloss writes with good humor about how, as a young American novelist, he rarely fit in. He kept orderly habits, and thus Norman Mailer’s parties, when he was invited to them, started too late for him. He tried to hang out at the [White Horse Tavern,](http://www.new-pony.com/tour/whitehorse.html "Information about White House Tavern") the writer’s bar in Greenwich Village, but was marked instantly as an outsider. “A registered Republican who was also listed in the [Social Register,](http://www.socialregisteronline.com/ "Social Register online")” he writes, “was something of a duck-billed platypus.”

Auchincloss’s memoir is discreet, yet bold-face names stride casually across its pages. At a dinner with his relative, the young Jacqueline Bouvier, in the 1950s, she praised his novel “Sybil,” about a dull girl.

Image![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/12/15/arts/sub-book/sub-book-jumbo.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&disable=upscale)

Louis AuchinclossCredit...Jerry Bauer

“Oh, you’ve written my life,” Bouvier said. “Respectable, middle-class, moderately well off. Accepted everywhere. Decent and dull.” A week later, Auchincloss writes, she broke her engagement to a man named Husted and a few years later married John F. Kennedy.

He writes that “the brilliant United States Supreme Court justice Antonin Scalia” argued in his presence that the true author of Shakespeare’s works was the Earl of Oxford. Auchincloss responds about Shakespeare: “To think his plays were written by Bacon or Oxford is, in my opinion, to show a tin ear.”

Throughout “A Voice from Old New York,” Auchincloss is trenchant about the faults of his class, but more often he defends it. “A common objection to inherited wealth is that it stifles the urge to work,” he writes. “I have not generally observed this to be true.”

He notes that many wealthy men of his acquaintance worked too hard, and should have left their fortunes to be managed by others. He quotes his father as saying about such men, “If they had been beachcombers, they’d be rich men today.”

He takes the measure of elite old families at about the end of the aughts: “It is commonly said that they have been relegated to the past. That is not so. They have simply lost their monopoly; they have had to move over and share their once closely guarded powers with the new rich, who are quite willing to spare the older generation so long as they are allowed to copy, and perhaps enhance, their style. See any Ralph Lauren ad.”

Auchincloss is hardest on himself in “A Voice from Old New York,” so much so that this memoir almost reads like a work of self-criticism that squirted out of Mao’s Cultural Revolution. He describes his early narcissism, his neglect of the poor and his casual anti-Semitism. He dabbled in larceny and vandalism, he tells us, and became briefly known at Groton as a snitch. He is quite honest about his fear while serving in the Navy during World War II.

Auchincloss grew up, and grew into himself, however. Some of the best writing in this book is about how he started writing, at Groton and at Yale and during stolen moments while in the military. His mother tried valiantly to stop him.

“She decided not only that I had no outstanding talent,” he writes, “but that my efforts showed a worldly streak that if published would make me look vulgar and hurt me with serious people in any career that I adopted.” Thus Auchincloss published his first novel, “The Indifferent Children,” under a pen name.

Auchincloss’s writing didn’t hurt him during his practice of law. “It was simply regarded as a curiosity,” he writes, “like a fondness for yoga.”

If he never stopped caring about what those in his own world thought of him, he found a deeper kind of true north. “Society matters not so much,” he writes here. “Words are everything.”

#### A VOICE FROM OLD NEW YORK

##### A Memoir of My Youth

By Louis Auchincloss

“Who was I to think I could change the face of American education?” asks the fictional Frank Prescott.

![Image 1: Book cover of The Rector of Justin](https://www.educationnext.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/sept20-blog-stoll-auchincloss-img01.png)The recent victory of [Jake Auchincloss](https://www.jakeforma.com/meet-jake) in a Massachusetts Democratic congressional primary inspired me to try reading one of the novels by the politician’s distant relative, Louis Auchincloss.

The [New York Times obituary of Louis Auchincloss](https://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/28/nyregion/28auchincloss.html), who died in 2010, said, “ ‘The Rector of Justin’ (1964), which was a best seller and a finalist for the National Book Award, is regarded by many critics as Mr. Auchincloss’s best and most important novel. Its protagonist is Frank Prescott, the headmaster of a New England boys’ school before the war, a man of intellect and idealism who could be noble, generous and kind but also, by turns, cruel, callous and arbitrary.”

Fifty-six years after its original publication, _The Rector of Justin_ holds up pretty well, at least in spots. At one point the Prescott character in the book says, “The older I get the more I realize that the only thing a teacher has to go on is that rare spark in a boy’s eye. And when you see _that_, Brian, you’re an ass if you worry where it comes from. Whether it’s an ode of Horace or an Icelandic saga or something that goes bang in a laboratory.”

That line made me smile because I recognized the insight from a couple of other recent _Education Next_ articles. [Reviewing Bernard Bailyn’s book Illuminating History: A Retrospective of Seven Decades](https://www.educationnext.org/education-of-bernard-bailyn-illuminating-history-book-review/), I wrote that Bailyn “credits Paul Buck, Harvard’s provost from 1945 to 1953. ‘From Buck I learned the basic requirement of good teaching: to somehow find the student’s instinctive, natural point of interest, encourage him or her to see its possibilities, and then leave the student alone to do what could be done.’”

![Image 2: Louis Auchincloss](https://www.educationnext.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/sept20-blog-stoll-auchincloss-img02.png)

Louis Auchincloss, author of _The Rector of Justin_

And in [a piece about Elbert Lenrow](https://www.educationnext.org/best-damn-class-i-ever-took-how-teaching-is-like-playing-piano-lenrow/), described by Nicholas Delbanco as “a great teacher,” I quoted Katherine H. Burkmann describing Lenrow’s methods: “his teaching involved encouragement: he was not in any way judgmental. He felt, he said, that the most important thing in presenting the literature to his young students was to get their reaction. …When students came to him for advice, he said, he helped them make their own decisions; he didn’t believe in pushing them.”

Later in _The Rector of Justin_, the Prescott character says, “There is no real distinction between the pulpit and the classroom. I tried to put God into every book and sport in Justin. That was my ideal, to spread a sense of his presence so that it would not be confined to prayers and sacred studies and to spread it in such a way as to make the school _joyful_.”

Elsewhere in the book, Prescott claims, “the greatness of the private school…is not that it produces geniuses—they grow anyway, and can’t be made—but that it can sometimes turn a third-rate student into a second-rate one. We can’t boast publicly of such triumphs, but they are still our glory.”

![Image 3: Jake Auchincloss](https://www.educationnext.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/sept20-blog-stoll-auchincloss-img03.png)

Jake Auchincloss, winner of a Massachusetts Democratic primary for a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, backs “choice in education with more charter schools.”

Prescott’s career ends not so much in glory as in humility. “Who was I to think I could change the face of American education?” he asks on his deathbed.

Perhaps the real politician Jake Auchincloss will have more success at such change than did Louis Auchincloss’s fictional character. The politician seems set to try. Jake Auchincloss [pledges](https://www.jakeforma.com/platform-of-opportunity) to “invest in human capital during the cognitively critical early years by expanding early childhood programs; during K–12 by deepening STEM instruction and by promoting choice in education with more charter schools; during and after secondary education by widening the access and accreditation of technical and vocational education; and during college by limiting student loans according to future income and streamlining the online path to a bachelor’s degree.”

“Choice in education” is a rare phrase these days among campaigning Democrats. It wasn’t a major issue in the hard-fought primary in the Massachusetts Fourth Congressional District now represented by Joseph P. Kennedy III. But if Jake Auchincloss stays with it, he may yet help more actual students experience the Frank Prescott-style dream of “make the school _joyful_.”

_Ira Stoll is managing editor of_ Education Next.

*   Dec. 4, 1964

NOW that Christmas is alarmingly near and the women of this country are doing all the thinking, planning, shop­ping and preparing for which the men never thank them enough, the time has come for the customary retrospective glance at the books of the year. What is the state of beautiful letters? How fare writers, pub­lishers and sellers of books in this year of economic affluence, political confusion and international turmoil?

The first question is unanswerable. Litera­ture, like certain paintings, is best judged from a distance. Some fine books were pub­lished in 1964. A great number of compe­tent and interesting books worth anybody's time today but probably not worth remem­bering in 1974 were published. And many books were published that represented trends, ideas, theories’ and tastes so controversial that no final verdicts are possible. One man's pornography is another man's serious pro­test. One woman's meaningless and tedious experiment in fictional technique is another woman's stimulating advance of the avant­garde.

As usual, some fine books failed to sell and some wretched books sold madly. Books in general sold so well that one novelist re­tired to a Greek island, another built a swimming pool on his country place and six publishers switched from 8-year‐old Scotch to 12-year‐old Scotch. The most popular novel of the year was a spy thriller by an unknown author, “The Spy Who Came in From the Cold” by John Le Carré. Many critics thought that the best novel of the year was “Herzog” by Saul Bellow, which is the leading best‐seller now. And the Nobel Prize for Literature, which often is awarded to an author of whom few people have ever heard, went to a world‐famous writer, Jean­Paul Sartre, who for reasons of his own refused it.

**Five Stood Out**

For many years at this time I have listed the 10 books of the previous 11 months that I admired most or enjoyed most. This year only five seem to me worth raising high above other good books. They are the following:

“The Story of a Life” by Konstantin Pau­stovsky, the best book by a Russian that I have read in 40 years, the autobiography of a master story‐teller who recalls his childhood and youth in a time of war and revolution with superlative skill and with a serenity of spirit almost noble.

“The Rector of Justin” by Louis Auchin­closs, in my opinion the best novel of the year, a subtle, ironic and compassionate story about a celebrated schoolmaster.

“Little Big Man” by Thomas Berger, a brilliant novel, about the Western frontier, Indian wars, gunmen, etc., written with im­mense gusto, cynical humor and absolute historical accuracy. ‘Not a spoof, as it has been erroneously labeled, but a synthesis of the Western experience.

“The Age of Triumph and Frustration: Modern Dialogues” by Charles Yost, a wise,

“The Italians” by Luigi Barzini, an astute Italian on the Italian national character, a dazzlingly clever book, so immensely en­tertaining that its shrewd insights are in some danger of being overlooked.

There were more good novels this year than last. Those who lament the low estate of modern fiction usually have not read enough of it, or have read only the books they profess to dislike. They ought to con­sider reading some of these: “The Rising of the. Lark” by Ann Moray, “Sing for Your Supper” by Pamela Frankau, “Reuben, Reu­ben” by Peter De Vries, “The Night of the Generals” by Hans Helmut Kirst, “The Keep­ers of the House” by Shirley Ann Grau, “An Honorable Estate” by Lane Kauffman, “The Rope Bridge” by Cecilie Leslie, and “Incog­nito” by Petru Dumitriu.

This year, as has been true for some time, several of the best novels were his­torical novels. These five are all outstandi ing: “The Constant Star” by Prudence An­drew, “The Land Breakers” by John Ehle, “Two Roads to Guadalupe” by Robert Lewis Taylor, “Tomorrow's Fire” by Jay Williams, and “The Grove of Eagles” by Winston Graham.

**Lack of Good Biographies**

There weren’t many good biographies this year, or else I missed them. “Henry of Na­varre” by Hesketh Pearson, who wrote a dozen or more urbane biographies, was ex­cellent. It was his last. Mr. Pearson died last April. A. L. Rowse's “William Shake­speare” was written with all the learning, grace and fiery conviction always present in Mr. Rowse's distinguished histories.

Works of history written with literary skill and intended for nonscholarly readers continued to flourish. Among the best were: “A Coffin for King Charles” by C. V. Wedg­wood, “When the Cheering Stopped: The Last Tears of Woodrow Wilson” by Gene Smith, “Paris in the Terror” by Stanley Loomis, “Russia at War: 1941-1945” by Alexander Werth, “The Golden Bees: The Story of the Bonapartes” by Theo Aronson, “The Great Indian Mutiny” by Richard Col­lier and “The Hundred Days” by Edith Saunders.

Another class of books in which many greatly talented writers specialize, travel and exploration, contained some of the most in­teresting works of the year: “A View of All the Russias” by Laurens van der Post, “The Great Red Island” by Arthur Stratton, “The Stone Age Island: New Guinea Today” by Maslyn Williams, “Arabia Felix” by Thor­kild Hansen, “A Traveller in Italy” by H. V. Morton and “Cooper's Creek” by Alan Moore­head.

No one, no matter how well intentioned, can read enough books. The shops are burst­ing with good ones I didn’t read, particu­larly those in classifications I don’t cus­tomarily find time for: sports, art, nature, humor, etc. Christmas shopping in a book store should be a pleasure this year.

_Each year for its Christmas Book Issue, the Book Review invites the men who make the hooks most peopie are reading to engage in a symposium on atopic of literary interest. In this year's symposium, the heads of firms whose books are on the current best‐setter list were asked: Among the books published by other houses in_ 1964, _which one do you wish ‘had been on your awn list—and whyf Their answers follow:_

Two books—I should really say two writers—take equal place as my preference for the. book I wish Atheneum had published in 1964: “Herzog” by Saul Bellow and “The Wapshot Scandal” by John Cheever.

The “whys” of ray choice are as similar as the books seem different.

Both books are mature, indeed resplendent expressions of the finest and most distinctive pens of our time. Both writers are men of surpassing gifts, artists of the highest order whose work is already, in their early middle years, assuming a place on the shelves of world literature. Gheever and Bellow are that rarest of gifts to a publisher and to a reader: writers for today and for tomorrow.

Periodically one finds that rare book which is exemplary for an entire field of writing. In “O Strange New World” Howard Mumford Jones has written such a work. A brilliant example of creative historical scholarship and one which testifies convincingly to the true relevance of the historian's craft—to give dimension and meaning to contemporary experience through a dramatic and profound sense of the past. And Jones can write so marvelously! He gives ideas and past events such color and life that what might have been for another writer a mere exercise in historical research becomes in his hands dramatic living narrative. “O Strange New World” is clearly the fruit of mature learning and wisdom; it reflects a profound sense of the human, an astonishing breadth of vision and a perennially youthful enthusiasm for the excitement of discovery.

I would have been happy to publish Charles Chaplin's “My Autobiography.” (Indeed I made an effort to obtain the American rights from the ‘British publisher the moment the book was announced, but alas, it was too late.) Not that the book is without major flaws: the sections dealing with Hollywood are disappointing in light of what one would have expected from Chaplin. But the early part .of the book describing the battle of the family against poverty is a masterpiece, and the sections dealing with the attempts of various groups in the United States, including even the Government, to humiliate a great artist offer a lesson for our times. In all, it is a book that will long be remembered, and the fact that it is selling very well certainly does not detract from its appeal

Over the years a great deal of nonsense has come to be written about the Irish. Alas, too often it has come from the Irish themselves. This blather tends to worsen when the subject is hyphenated, to Irish‐American. Bill Shannon, however, has gene a long way, in his; brilliant, compassionate but sturdily objective study of “The American Irish” to clear away forever not only the ancient “Pat and Mike” stereotypes but the more modern Fifth‐Avenue St. Patrick's Day “professional” Irish bathos as well. Shannon pierces to the heart of the heroic story Of an ethnic minority who rose—in little less than a hundred years—from second‐class citizenship to place. a President in the White House. The book charts the evolution of the Irish from immigration to assimilation not only politically but economically, culturally and spiritually. And he understands the psychic cost of hacking out an identity—as well as a living. He can even explain what makes John O’Hara tick.

Any publisher in his right mind would like to have had “The Spy Who Came in From the Cold” on his list,’ but, of all the 1964 best‐sellers, the one I covet most is Saul Bellow's “Herzog.” The publisher bringing out such a book has the satisfaction of knowing he is living up to. the fullest extent of his personal commitment. He is putting into the hands of people who both read and think a book that illuminates the experience of life. He is spending his firm's resources to publish a book of enduring value. He is brightening his list with the work of an author who is an inspiration to other authors and, therefore, a priceless asset to the house. He is caught up in the euphoria of the happiest of publishing experiences, issuing a good book that makes his imprint a little bit prouder than it was before—and one that is also a popular success.

Of all the books published in 1964, “A Moveable Feast” by Ernest Hemingway had the most private meaning for me because it brought back the days some decades ago when I was assistant editor of Esquire magazine and Hemingway was sending editor Arnold Gingrich monthly stories and articles via African courier or inland waterway or whatever mode of transport seemed most appropriate.

The high point came when he sent Cosmopolitan the'story he had written for us because their deadline was earlier, and then sent us their story a few weeks later. They got “The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber” and we got “The Snows of Killimanjaro.” How can you lose with a genius of the Underwood?

But I also enjoyed “A Movable Feast” on its own merits —for its flawless style (an ever‐increasing rarity these days) and its evocation of a place and time and mood that will remain forever ours because of this book.

I wish we‐had published Louis Auchincloss's “The Rector of Justin.”

One becomes absorbed in the characters of this novel and in what happens to them: The Rector in particular is unforgettable. A complicated man with a passionate nature who at the same time possesses understanding and a sense of humor. He is a person who creates drama around him, and the author develops this with great power and effectiveness.

This fine novel is the work of a sophisticated and civilized writer who brings brilliance and erudition to the dialogue between his characters.

Dag Hammarskjold's “Markings” is a book I would have beerf most happy to have on the Houghton Mifflin list. It is an unusual personal document, all the more unexpected because it comes from one who must have found it very difficult to snatch time for this kind of contemplation.

Admirers of Hammarskjold's talent and success story will be surprised that for so many years he lived with uncertainty, that he felt an almost overpowering need for more assurance of the meaning of life. And they will be heartened that he appeared to be able to change the focus of Bis attention from despair over himself to faith in God, to find a certain serenity in his commitment to a life of selfless service to humanity.

Here is an admirable study in enlightened introspection, complemented by a sensitive translation by Leif Sjoberg and W. H. Auden and by Auden's utterly honest and perceptive Foreword. !

Although current publishing mores seem to de‐emphasize the traditional dishonor connected with a strong expression of interest in another publisher's author, I am still apprehensive over my assignment. However, in the spirit of cooperation. I must confess my admiration for Robert Lowell's “For the Union Dead.” For sheer power and substance Lowell's verse is unexcelled. As a student of history I am particularly Impressed with his historical range and perspective. Moreover, the flexible form of composition he employs is more meaningful to the general reader and will serve to restore poetry to its rightful position in the world of books.

First, Paustovsky's. “The Story of a Life,” a long and absorbing book. In Joseph Barnes's translation its style is delightful. In a time of need last summer it kept my mind off politics and our withering drought in Connecticut.

Next, fudging a bit, I nominate “Rie Birth of Western Civilization” edited by Michael Grant. Though our imprint is on the U. S. edition, this book was actually published by Thames and Hudson of London. It is magnificent in concept, in format, in style of illustration and printing. Its text is crisp and authoritative. I wish its aggregate quality could be more of ten matched on this side of the Atlantic.

Last, the new edition of Merriam's “Webster's Collegiate Dictionary.” To me this is a particularly illuminating piece of nonfiction because I am a bad speller.. But I can figure real good (permitted current usage here, of course), and I figure this would have been a dandy book for our list this year or any other.

I would like to have published Robert Lowell's “For the Union Dead” because of the extraordinary brilliance and quality of Lowell's talent in general, and because New American Library would like to include major American poets, established or genuinely promising, in its small but growing trade list. Lowell is a true poet who will last, and one whose language and style are equal to his fiercely imaginative vision. In a day and age when such a large premium is put on ephemeral best sellers one would like to be identified with the recognizable mainstream of enduring American literature.

The book I’d pick is Charlton Hinman's “The Printing and Proofreading of the First Folio of Shakespeare” because it is a work of creative scholarship whose influence will steadily grow, with the result that we shall come closer to what Shakespeare actually wrote than we have been at any time in the past 400 years. **WALTER J. MONTON**

Certainly the book published in 1964 by a house other than Putnam's which I wish had been on my list is Hubert Selby Jr.'s “Last Exit to Brooklyn.” I bought not one” but two copies (in itself an unusual eventpublishers just don’t buy books), as ihe result of an advertisement in The New York Times run by the Doubleday Book Shops for the publisher, Grove Press.

I was immediately struck by Mr. Selby's moral values, his skillfully drawn picture of the nether regions of New York, and, above all, by his sheer _joie de vivre._ Truly it's a book I‐wish we at Putnam's had published.

I have decided to be completely honest in my reply. The outside book that I wish most sincerely had been published by us is the one that _sold the moat copies!_—with the only restriction that it had to be a book that I would not be ashamed to see on our Random House list. I think that last restricting clause is particularly necessary Jn a year that has seen the publication of some books that, in . my opinion, are simply inexcusable.

If you will look up your highly respected New York Times best‐seller lists, therefore, you will be able to determine for yourself the book that I would select for your symposium.

During the year we try our best not to covet ourneighbors's books although at times the temptation to break this particular commandment becomes pretty strong. I will confess wishing we had published one absolutely splendid book, “The Rector of Justin,” by. Louis Auchincloss. I am told that it appeared in one newspaper's best‐seller list as having been written by Ernest Hemingway and I’m afraid that's the closest we came to publishing it!

Among the books published in 1964, and not published by S&S, the one which I wish had been on our list is: “Russia at War, 1941-1945” by Alexander Werth.

My reason: Because it does for the Russian participation in World War II what “The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich” did for Nazi Germany. William L. Shirer's tribute to Werth's magnificent book makes it “must,” top priority reading for me. This is what history looks like when it is poured red hot from the ladle.
